title: Week 2 — Grammar of Graphics & Design Principles
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Every chart is a set of choices about how to map data variables onto visual properties: position, length, angle, color, size, shape. The “grammar of graphics” makes these choices explicit and composable, so that instead of memorizing chart types you can reason about encodings. This is the conceptual engine behind seaborn and Altair, and understanding it lets you build the right chart for a question rather than the nearest template.
But a correct encoding is not automatically an effective one. Perceptual research — from Cleveland and McGill’s experiments on how accurately people read different channels, to Gestalt principles of grouping, to preattentive features — tells us that some encodings are read quickly and accurately while others mislead. A graduate-level visualizer treats these findings as design constraints, not decoration.

💻 Live Code

Seaborn multi-encoding

import seaborn as sns
import plotly.express as px
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

tips = px.data.tips()
sns.scatterplot(
    data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip",
    hue="day", style="time", size="size",
)
plt.title("Four channels at once: position (x/y), color (day), shape (time), size (party)")
plt.show()








How many channels can you read at once before the chart becomes cluttered? Note how quickly the eye picks up position compared to size or shape.


The same relationship, one channel at a time

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", hue="day", ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Third variable as COLOR")
sns.scatterplot(data=tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", size="size", ax=axes[1], legend=False)
axes[1].set_title("Third variable as SIZE")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()










Altair grammar (chart spec)
Altair builds an interactive chart specification. The object is created here; in a notebook or rendered Altair output it displays as an interactive chart.

import altair as alt

chart = (
    alt.Chart(tips)
    .mark_point()
    .encode(x="total_bill", y="tip", color="day", shape="time")
)
chart

title: Week 1 — Foundations & Setup
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Data visualization in a graduate data-science context is more than making charts — it is the craft of turning data of many shapes into understanding. This course is organized around the idea that “complex data” comes in distinct modalities: tabular tables, time series, networks, text, images, and geographic data. Each has its own structure, its own failure modes, and its own visual vocabulary. Before we can visualize any of them well, we need a shared foundation: a reliable Python environment, the habit of working with tidy data, and a clear sense of what good visualization is for.
This week also introduces the tool that distinguishes this course from a notebook-only workflow: Streamlit. Rather than ending each project as a static rendered document, you will increasingly build small interactive applications. We start gently — a “hello world” app — so that the tool is familiar long before the client–server work later in the term.

title: Week 3 — Tabular & Multivariate Data
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Tabular data — rows of observations, columns of variables — is the most common shape data takes, and it is deceptively hard to visualize well once the number of variables grows. A handful of columns can be shown with bars, scatterplots, and small multiples. But real datasets often have dozens of variables, and the challenge becomes seeing structure: which variables move together, which observations cluster, where the outliers are.
This week builds wrangling fluency, then moves to multivariate visualization: pair plots, correlation heatmaps, and PCA. We treat PCA not as a statistics lecture but as a visualization tool — a way to project many dimensions down to two so the eye can see grouping that no single pairwise plot reveals. PCA reappears conceptually in the embedding work of Week 13.

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(wine.data)   # standardize first!
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
pcs = pca.fit_transform(X)

plt.figure()
scatter = plt.scatter(pcs[:, 0], pcs[:, 1], c=wine.target, cmap="Set2")

Notice that no single pairwise plot of the 13 features would separate the cultivars this cleanly — PCA finds the directions that do.


Wrap into a Streamlit app (copy-and-run)
# app.py  —  run with:  streamlit run app.py
import streamlit as st
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import pandas as pd

wine = load_wine(as_frame=True)
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(wine.data)
pcs = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X)
plot_df = pd.DataFrame(pcs, columns=["PC1", "PC2"])
plot_df["cultivar"] = wine.target.astype(str)

st.title("Wine PCA Explorer")
st.scatter_chart(plot_df, x="PC1", y="PC2", color="cultivar")

title: Week 4 — Time-Series Data
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Time-series data carries an extra structural fact that ordinary tabular data does not: order. Observations are linked by their position in time, so patterns like trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation become the story. Visualizing time well means respecting that order — choosing the right temporal resolution, handling gaps, and deciding whether to show raw values, smoothed trends, or rates of change.
Time is also where some of the most common visual dishonesty appears: truncated y-axes that exaggerate change, mismatched aspect ratios, and dual-axis charts that imply spurious relationships. This week pairs the mechanics of temporal visualization with a discipline of honest communication, and introduces uncertainty visualization — error bars, confidence bands, and intervals — since real time series are rarely as precise as a single line implies. Uncertainty returns in Week 13 when we visualize model predictions.

We use the Mauna Loa atmospheric CO₂ series (ships with statsmodels): a textbook example of a strong upward trend with clear annual seasonality.

Load and resample

import statsmodels.api as sm

co2 = sm.datasets.co2.load_pandas().data.dropna()
monthly = co2["co2"].resample("MS").mean().dropna()
print("Span:", monthly.index.min().date(), "to", monthly.index.max().date())
monthly.head()

Span: 1958-03-01 to 2001-12-01


1958-03-01    316.100000
1958-04-01    317.200000
1958-05-01    317.433333
1958-07-01    315.625000
1958-08-01    314.950000
Name: co2, dtype: float64




Trend via a rolling mean

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ax = monthly.plot(alpha=0.4, label="monthly", figsize=(9, 4))
monthly.rolling(12).mean().plot(ax=ax, label="12-month rolling mean", linewidth=2)
ax.set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)")
ax.set_title("Mauna Loa CO₂: raw monthly vs. smoothed trend")
ax.legend()
plt.show()










Uncertainty band

roll = monthly.rolling(12)
mean, std = roll.mean(), roll.std()

ax = mean.plot(figsize=(9, 4), label="12-mo mean")
ax.fill_between(mean.index, mean - 2 * std, mean + 2 * std, alpha=0.2, label="±2σ band")
ax.set_ylabel("CO₂ (ppm)")
ax.set_title("Trend with an uncertainty band")
ax.legend()
plt.show()










Seasonal decomposition

from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose

result = seasonal_decompose(monthly, period=12)
result.plot()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








The decomposition separates the long-run trend, the repeating annual seasonal cycle, and the residual — three views that a single line would blur together.


Wrap into a Streamlit app (copy-and-run)
# app.py  —  run with:  streamlit run app.py
import streamlit as st
import statsmodels.api as sm

co2 = sm.datasets.co2.load_pandas().data.dropna()
freq = st.selectbox("Resolution", {"Monthly": "MS", "Quarterly": "QS", "Yearly": "YS"})
series = co2["co2"].resample({"Monthly": "MS", "Quarterly": "QS", "Yearly": "YS"}[freq]).mean()

st.title("CO₂ Trend Explorer")
st.line_chart(series)

title: Week 5 — Building Interactive Apps with Streamlit
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
A notebook is a great place to develop a visualization, but a poor place to deliver one to someone who isn’t a programmer. Streamlit closes that gap: with a few lines of pure Python, a script becomes an interactive web app with widgets, layout, and live-updating charts. For a data-science course, this is more than convenience — it is the difference between a static figure and a tool someone can explore.
This week is deliberately tooling-heavy. We cover Streamlit’s execution model (the script re-runs top-to-bottom on every interaction), the widget set, layout primitives (columns, tabs, sidebar), and — crucially — caching, which is what keeps an app responsive when it loads data or fits a model. We also deploy a first app to the web. Everything after this week assumes Streamlit fluency: the modality modules end in small apps, and the final project is a deployed client–server Streamlit application. Getting comfortable now is what makes the client–server weeks (11–13) feasible in a two-hour block.

title: Week 6 — Graph & Network Data
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Much of the most interesting data in the world is relational: who follows whom, which papers cite which, how proteins interact, how money or messages flow. This data does not fit neatly into rows and columns — its meaning lives in the connections. A network (or graph) represents this directly as a set of nodes joined by edges, and visualizing it well lets us see structure that a table would hide: clusters, hubs, bridges, and bottlenecks.
Network visualization is also where good design principles get tested hardest. Unlike a scatterplot, where position carries clear meaning, a node-link diagram’s layout is the output of an algorithm, and different layout algorithms can make the same graph look completely different. Position no longer maps to a data variable; it maps to a force-simulation’s idea of “closeness.” This is powerful but treacherous — a “hairball” of thousands of overlapping edges can look impressive and communicate nothing. This week we learn to choose layouts deliberately, encode structural properties (like centrality and community) onto visual channels, and know when a node-link diagram is the wrong tool and a matrix or aggregated view would serve better.
This builds directly on the encoding and perception principles from Weeks 2 and 5, and the techniques here recur later when we visualize embeddings (Week 13), which are themselves a way of laying out relational similarity in space.

Draw with a layout, encode degree and community
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import networkx as nx

# Community detection (greedy modularity)
from networkx.algorithms.community import greedy_modularity_communities
communities = list(greedy_modularity_communities(G))
color_map = {}
for cid, comm in enumerate(communities):
    for node in comm:
        color_map[node] = cid

pos = nx.spring_layout(G, seed=42)          # force-directed
node_sizes = [degrees[n] * 80 for n in G.nodes()]
node_colors = [color_map[n] for n in G.nodes()]

nx.draw_networkx(
    G, pos,
    node_size=node_sizes,
    node_color=node_colors,
    cmap=plt.cm.Set2,
    edge_color="#cccccc",
    with_labels=False,
)
plt.axis("off")
plt.show()

title: Week 7 — Text Data
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Text is the least visually obvious modality: it has no natural x and y, no inherent shape. To visualize it we must first transform it into something countable or geometric — token frequencies, document-term structures, topic distributions, or high-dimensional embeddings. Each transformation makes a different aspect of the text visible, and each carries assumptions worth examining.
The popular word cloud is a useful cautionary tale: it is eye-catching but encodes word importance on the perceptually weak channels of area and position-by-layout-algorithm, so it communicates far less than a simple sorted bar chart. This week we treat text visualization seriously: frequency and keyness done honestly, topic models (BERTopic) to summarize a corpus, and embedding projections (with UMAP, previewed here and revisited in Week 13) to lay documents out by semantic similarity. The throughline is that text visualization is really the visualization of a model’s view of text — so understanding the transform is as important as the picture.

text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Images are dense, high-dimensional data: a single modest photo is hundreds of thousands of numbers. Visualizing image data therefore splits into two related tasks. The first is making collections legible — montages, grids, and summaries that let you scan a dataset, spot label errors, and understand class balance, all of which matter enormously before any modeling. The second is visualizing what happens inside an image model: which pixels a classifier attends to, what intermediate feature maps look like, where a model is confidently wrong.
This is one of the most data-science-oriented weeks, because visualization here is a debugging and explanation tool, not decoration. A saliency or attention map overlaid on an image can reveal that a “dog detector” is actually keying on grassy backgrounds. We treat image visualization as a window into both data quality and model behavior, which connects directly to the ML/NLP visualization module in Week 13 and to the explanation needs of the final project.

title: Week 9 — Map Visualization — Module I
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Geographic data is special because location is both the key and a source of distortion. The Earth is a sphere; a map is flat; every projection that flattens it lies in some way — about area, shape, distance, or direction. A choropleth that looks authoritative can mislead badly if it ignores projection, uses raw counts where rates are needed, or bins values carelessly. So before any pretty map, this module establishes the unglamorous foundations: coordinate reference systems (CRS), projections and what each preserves, and spatial joins that attach data to geometry.
We then build the core static thematic maps — choropleths, dot-density, and hex/bin maps — with geopandas, mapclassify, and contextily. The emphasis is on honesty: choosing rates over counts, classifying values defensibly, and picking projections suited to the question. This grounding sets up Module II next week, where the same data becomes interactive and lands inside a Streamlit dashboard.

title: Week 10 — Map Visualization — Module II
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Static maps answer a fixed question; interactive maps let users ask their own. For geographic data — where users almost always want to zoom to their region, hover for exact values, or toggle layers — interactivity is often what makes a map useful rather than merely decorative. This module builds on the cartographic foundations from Module I and adds the web layer: tile-based interactive maps with folium (Leaflet) and plotly, and the patterns for embedding them in a Streamlit app.
The deeper goal is the geospatial dashboard: a coordinated view where a map, a filter, and a chart update together. This is the first time the course combines a modality with full interactivity in an app, and it is direct preparation for the final project, where a Streamlit client will display model output that may itself be geographic. We also confront performance — interactive maps with many features can choke a browser — and the design discipline of not drowning the user in layers and popups.

title: Week 11 — Consuming APIs & Data Endpoints
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Until now, every app has been self-contained: the data and any computation live inside the Streamlit script. Real data-science applications rarely work that way. Data lives behind APIs, and models run on servers — separate processes, often on separate machines — that the front-end talks to over HTTP. Separating the client (the app the user sees) from the server (where data and models live) is what lets a visualization scale, stay secure, and reuse a model across many front-ends.
This week is deliberately client-only: we learn the request/response pattern by consuming endpoints that already exist, so the networking concepts land before we add the complexity of writing a server. You will hit public REST APIs and a small provided course endpoint, parse JSON responses into pandas, handle errors and latency gracefully, and visualize what comes back inside Streamlit. Next week (12) you build the server side; the week after (13) you visualize live model output. Think of these three weeks as one arc: consume → serve → visualize.

r = requests.get(
    "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",

Example B — robust call with caching
import streamlit as st, requests

@st.cache_data(ttl=300)
def fetch(url, params=None):
    r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()        # raises on 4xx/5xx
    return r.json()

try:
    payload = fetch("https://api.restcountries.com/v3.1/all")
except requests.HTTPError as e:
    st.error(f"Request failed: {e}")
    payload = None


Client app skeleton
# app.py
import streamlit as st, requests, pandas as pd

st.title("API Client")
lat = st.number_input("Latitude", value=38.9)
lon = st.number_input("Longitude", value=-77.0)

if st.button("Fetch"):
    try:
        r = requests.get("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
                         params={"latitude": lat, "longitude": lon, "hourly": "temperature_2m"},
                         timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()

        df = pd.DataFrame({"time": pd.to_datetime(h["time"]), "temp": h["temperature_2m"]})
        st.line_chart(df.set_index("time"))
    except Exception as e:

title: Week 12 — Serving Models with FastAPI / Flask
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
Last week you consumed endpoints that someone else built. This week you become that someone. Serving a model means taking a trained estimator — a scikit-learn classifier, say — and putting it behind a small web server so that any client can send it inputs and receive predictions over HTTP. This is the standard way models are deployed in practice: the model lives in one place, and many front-ends (web apps, mobile apps, other services) consume it through a stable API.
We use FastAPI as the primary framework (with Flask shown as the lightweight alternative) because it is fast to write, validates inputs automatically, and generates interactive documentation for free. The work is mostly about interface design: what does a prediction request look like, what does the response contain, how do you load the model once rather than on every request, and how do you handle bad input. Crucially, this week is scaffolded — you start from a provided trained model and a skeleton server — so the two hours go to the meaningful parts (request/response design, testing the endpoint) rather than boilerplate. Next week, your Streamlit client from Week 11 connects to this server, and you visualize what it returns.

title: Week 12 — Serving Models with FastAPI / Flask
text:
💻 Notebook / App Snippets

FastAPI model-serving endpoint
# app.py  —  run with:  uvicorn app:app --reload
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel
import joblib, numpy as np

app = FastAPI()
model = joblib.load("model.joblib")          # load ONCE at startup

class Features(BaseModel):
    flipper_length_mm: float
    body_mass_g: float

@app.post("/predict")
def predict(x: Features):
    X = np.array([[x.flipper_length_mm, x.body_mass_g]])
    pred = model.predict(X)[0]
    proba = model.predict_proba(X)[0].max()
    return {"prediction": str(pred), "confidence": float(proba)}


Flask alternative (same idea)
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import joblib, numpy as np

app = Flask(__name__)
model = joblib.load("model.joblib")

@app.post("/predict")
def predict():
    data = request.get_json()
    X = np.array([[data["flipper_length_mm"], data["body_mass_g"]]])
    return jsonify(prediction=str(model.predict(X)[0]))


Test the endpoint
import requests
r = requests.post("http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict",
                  json={"flipper_length_mm": 200, "body_mass_g": 4200}, timeout=5)
print(r.status_code, r.json())

title: Week 13 — ML/NLP Visualization
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
A trained model is a black box until you visualize it. This module is the payoff of the course’s data-science orientation: it brings together the modality skills (text, images, tabular) and the client–server plumbing (Weeks 11–12) to explain machine-learning models visually. We cover the standard explanatory visuals — feature importance, confusion matrices, ROC and precision–recall curves, embedding projections (UMAP, building on Weeks 3 and 7) — and the discipline of communicating model uncertainty rather than a single confident number.
The distinctive piece is wiring it together. The Streamlit client you wrote in Week 11 now calls the FastAPI model server you wrote in Week 12, sends real inputs, and visualizes the live response: the prediction, its confidence, and supporting explanation. This completes the consume → serve → visualize arc and is precisely the architecture the final project requires. By the end of the week you will have a working, end-to-end application in which a user interacts with a front-end that talks to a model behind an API and renders the result.

title: Week 14 — Deployment, Ethics & Final Workshop
text:
📖 Background & Motivation
A data-science application that only runs on your laptop isn’t finished. This module closes the loop by deploying the complete client–server system — the Streamlit front-end and the model-serving backend — so that anyone with the URL can use it. Deployment surfaces real concerns the local environment hides: configuration and secrets, cold starts and latency, how the client finds the server, and reproducibility so a grader (or a future you) can run it.
The week also steps back to the ethics of the whole enterprise. Across the term we have seen how easily visualizations mislead — truncated axes, count-vs-rate choropleths, hairball networks, decorative word clouds, overconfident model outputs. Here we make that explicit: distortion and manipulation, the false authority of a polished chart, bias and accessibility, and the special responsibilities of putting a model’s output in front of users who may over-trust it. The remainder of the session is a workshop: you present prototypes, give and receive structured critique, and leave with a concrete plan to finish the final project.

title: Visualization of Complex Data
text:
Welcome
This is the course book for DATS 6401 — Visualization of Complex Data, a graduate course at the George Washington University.
The course is organized around data modalities — the idea that “complex data” comes in distinct shapes (tabular, time-series, networks, text, images, geographic), each with its own visualization challenges. It is delivered through Streamlit, and builds toward a full client–server machine-learning application in which an interactive front-end communicates with a model served behind an API.

title: Visualization of Complex Data
text:
How this book works
Each chapter corresponds to one two-hour class session that interleaves concept lecture with hands-on work. Within a chapter you’ll find background and motivation, learning objectives, readings, a session outline with timings, code, an in-class activity, and homework.
A note on the code in this book:

In the Foundations chapters (Weeks 1–4), the Python code is executable — the charts you see were generated by running the code on this page. You can copy it and run it yourself; it uses datasets that ship with the libraries, so nothing needs to be downloaded.
From Week 5 onward, much of the code builds Streamlit apps and FastAPI/Flask servers. That code cannot run inside a static web page (a Streamlit app is a running server, not a chart). It is shown as copy-and-run source for your own environment, and where an app has been deployed, the live app is embedded directly in the page.

title: Visualization of Complex Data
text:
Course arc

Weeks 1–4 — Foundations. Setup, the grammar of graphics and perception, then the two conventional modalities (tabular/multivariate with PCA, and time-series with uncertainty).
Week 5 — The hinge: Streamlit. Everything after this is delivered as an app.
Weeks 6–10 — Complex modalities. Networks, text, images, and the two-part map module.
Weeks 11–13 — The client–server arc. Consume an endpoint → serve a model (FastAPI/Flask) → visualize live ML/NLP output.
Week 14 — Deploy, reflect, ship. Deploy the full system, confront visualization ethics, and workshop the final project.
